Setup was simple: the vendor, Larkspur Education Systems, installed all 32 units in two afternoons and trained staff in a single ninety-minute session. Battery life averages eleven hours, which comfortably covers a full school day. The interface syncs with our existing Skyward student records, and 98.6 percent of entries matched the office's manual cross-check. Parents receive absence texts within five minutes of the bell, and office calls about unexplained absences fell by roughly a third. The per-unit price of $219 fits within the $8,000 technology line approved for this school year. During a March audit, we found that the tablets store student names, home addresses, and guardian phone numbers unencrypted in local memory, and two units reported missing from classrooms have not been recovered. Teachers rated their satisfaction at 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-pilot survey. I recommend presenting the results to the principals' council on April 18.

This review covers the Halvorsen RoadMend 300 spray-injection patcher, which Eastport Public Works trialed from March through May. On 14 April the hydraulic boom arm cracked at its main weld and fell onto the roof of the support truck cab, missing the operator by less than a meter. Over the trial's 31 working days, the crew filled 1,860 potholes, averaging 60 per shift against our target of 45. Aggregate use came to 11 kilograms per patch, about 8 percent below our current method. All six operators were comfortable with the touchscreen controls after two days of training. Fuel consumption averaged 9 liters per hour, matching the vendor's specification. The purchase price is $148,000, and Halvorsen offers a 24-month service contract at $6,200 per year. Overall, the RoadMend is fast, economical with material, and easy to learn, and we recommend extending the trial through the summer on the Route 9 resurfacing corridor.

The hull was found in good condition, with paint thickness readings averaging 312 microns against a target of 300. Both main engines ran smoothly through a two-hour sea trial, and fuel consumption came in at 187 litres per hour, slightly below the budgeted 195. The passenger deck, including all 412 seats and the accessibility ramps, passed the cleanliness and fittings check without remarks. Galley staff completed their food hygiene recertification last month, and the records are up to date. The ship's lifejackets were counted at 470, which covers full capacity plus the required spares. During the vehicle deck check, the surveyors found that the bow door hydraulic seal was leaking and that the door could not be fully locked in the closed position. The crew's evacuation drill took six minutes and forty seconds, comfortably inside the eight-minute limit. The next scheduled inspection is set for 20 June, and Ms Vasquez will circulate the full measurement sheets to the operations office by Friday.
